fields.Electoral Act:
Section 72 (1) Subject to the provisions of this section, the place where a person resides within New Zealand at any material time or during any material period shall be determined for the purposes of this Act by reference to the facts of the case. (2)... a person can reside in one place only. (3) A person resides at the place where that person chooses to make his or her home by reason of family or personal relations, or for other domestic or personal reasons.
Section 74 (c) that electoral district— (i) is the last in which that person has continuously resided for a period equalling or exceeding 1 month; or (ii) where that person has never resided continuously in any one electoral district for a period equalling or exceeding 1 month, is the electoral district in which that person resides or has last resided.
(2) If a writ has been issued for an election, every person is treated, for the purposes of subsection (1)(c), as having completed a period of 1 month’s continuous residence in an electoral district if the person— (a) resides in the electoral district at the close of registration; and (b) would, if they continued to reside in the electoral district until the close of polling day, have continuously resided in the electoral district for a period equalling or exceeding 1 month.

issue: What happens when someone is on the dormant roll?

fields.Author: M
fields.Electoral Commission website:
The dormant roll is the roll voters get placed onto when we have not been able to contact them at their registered address. Voters remain on the electoral roll while we try to contact them through email, text or an alternate address if we have this information. After four weeks, if we haven’t heard from the voter (they have not updated their details) they will be moved to the dormant roll. Being on the dormant roll doesn’t change your roll type (general or Māori) or your electorate. Anyone who has updated their details since being made dormant is added back onto the main roll. Someone on the dormant roll is still eligible to vote, but if their current address is in a different electorate to their enrolled address, they may only be able to make a party vote. 
To get off the dormant roll, you simply need to update your enrolment address. However you need to do this before voting starts on 26 October 2026. You won’t be able to do it at the voting place. To check or update your enrolment details, go to vote.nz or call 0800 36 76 56. 
https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview > https://elections.nz/assets/2026-General-Election/2026-Factsheet-Make-Sure-Youre-Enrolled-for-the-2026-General-Election-v2.pdf
fields.Electoral Act:
Section 109 (1) The Electoral Commission must maintain a dormant roll that shows for each district the particulars of those persons whose names have been removed from the roll for the relevant district— (a) under section 89G; or (b) as a result of the removal of the name of that person from the roll under section 95A(4) or 96(4).
(2) The Electoral Commission must remove the name of a person from the dormant roll on the first occurrence of any of the following events:
(a) in the case of a person whose name has been removed from the electoral roll under section 89G, when the person registers as an elector of any district; or
(b) in the case of a person whose name has been removed from the electoral roll under section 95A(4) or section 96(4), when the person registers as an elector of any district; or (ba) in the case of a person whose name has been removed from the electoral roll under section 89G, 95A(4), or 96(4), when the person is registered as an elector of any district on the initiative of the Electoral Commission under section 89CB; or (c) in the case of a person who dies, when the Electoral Commission is satisfied of the identity of the person and the death has been notified to the Electoral Commission...
(d) the expiration of the period of 3 years beginning with the date on which the person’s name was placed on the dormant roll.
Section 89G - ...Elector cannot be contacted (whether by post, courier, or otherwise) is to be included on dormant roll
If this section applies, the Electoral Commission must— (a) make any inquiry as to the whereabouts of the elector that the Electoral Commission thinks fit; and (b) if the Electoral Commission is unable to contact the elector, remove the name of the elector from the roll and include the name on the dormant roll maintained under section 109.

fields.Author: M
fields.Electoral Commission website:
The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for Māori about which electoral roll to be on: the Māori roll or the general roll.
The Electoral Amendment Act, passed in 1975, defined Māori as a person of New Zealand Māori descent. It means anyone who is Māori has the option of enrolling to vote on either roll. 
Before 1975 your electoral roll was determined by the percentage of Māori blood you were deemed to have.
The Electoral Act 1993 linked the number of Māori electorates to population and Māori roll data, resulting in an increase in the number of Māori electorates.
In 2022 legislation was passed creating a continuous option. Instead of a 4-month Option period, Māori who are enrolled to vote can now change rolls at any time except in the three months before an election.
https://vote.nz/maori-enrolment/resources/resources/history-of-the-maori-electoral-option
Your roll choice affects which candidates you can choose from in parliamentary elections and local elections. It also helps determine the number of Māori and general electorates.
The roll you choose decides which electorate you vote in and who you can vote for to represent you in Parliament.
If you choose the Māori roll, you will vote for a candidate in the Māori electorate you live in.
If you choose the general roll, you will vote for a candidate in the general electorate you live in.
You will vote for the same list of political parties in a general election, whichever roll you choose to be on.
The number of Māori on the general and Māori rolls, together with the results of the census, are used to work out the number of general and Māori electorates. The number of Māori enrolled on the Māori roll could mean the number of Māori electorates increases, decreases, or stays the same for future elections. There are currently seven Māori electorates and 65 general electorates. 
https://vote.nz/maori-enrolment/about-the-option/about/what-does-your-choice-mean-for-you
